Working from the article text provided directly. Here is the full analysis:

Published online:
    September 4, 2026

Geographic focus:
    Global (primary focus: United States, with material coverage of Japan, Germany, Venezuela, Middle East)

Temporal focus:
    T1. Historical report [YES] — recaps the past week's market moves
    T2. Forward-looking reporting short-term risks (next few weeks/months) [YES] — fuel prices into midterms, bond volatility, Treasury market structure risk
    T3. Forward-looking reporting long-term risks (next quarters/years) [YES] — Venezuela oil deal (100-year lease), structural shift in Treasury ownership, AI chip revenue forecasts

Synopsis:
    A five-theme weekly wrap. Global sovereign bond yields are surging — US 10Y at highest since Jan 2025, Japan 10Y above 3% for first time since 1996, German Bund at 15-year highs — driven by rising real yields, not just inflation expectations, making the move potentially persistent. The marginal buyer in the $29T Treasury market has shifted from price-insensitive central banks to leveraged hedge funds (now holding $2.6T, 8%+ of market), raising systemic fragility. Trump unveiled a Venezuela oil deal (35% US stake, 100-year lease, 65B barrels) amid colonialism accusations and legal/political risks. Brent crude topping $95/bbl and rising pump prices threaten to dominate the midterm election narrative. Broadcom missed Q4 guidance despite a Q3 beat, dragging AVGO shares lower in a high-bar AI chip environment.

Q01. Is the content's main message on the US economy, US yields, US interest rates?
Relevance: YES — The bond/yield theme is the lead story and most extensively covered, directly implicating US rates, Treasury market structure, and macro conditions.

Q05. Focus on the very latest information: What is the sentiment/tone including the very latest information on US interest rates?
Sentiment: 75 (on a scale of -100 [More dovish than before] to 100 [More hawkish than before])

The tone is firmly hawkish: traders are "bracing for rate hikes around the world this month," real yields (not just inflation expectations) are driving the selloff — a stickier, more structurally entrenched dynamic — and the shift to leveraged fast-money as marginal Treasury buyer amplifies the risk of a disorderly further selloff. No dovish counterweight is offered anywhere in the piece.
